C004.subject: Policy effectiveness
C004.object: contradictory studies are meta-analyzed using a shared causal model that controls for contextual confounders
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Policy effectiveness contradictory studies are meta-analyzed using a shared causal model that controls for contextual confounders]

[PATH:empirical] Systematic review of meta-analyses in social policy that compare traditional meta-analytic methods (e.g., random-effects) with causal-model-based meta-analyses controlling for contextual confounders, focusing on consistency of effect estimates across contradictory studies. — Directly tests whether a shared causal model reduces or resolves contradictions in policy effectiveness findings, providing confirmatory or refutatory evidence for the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Simulation studies that generate synthetic data with known policy effects and varying degrees of confounding, then compare the accuracy and convergence of meta-analyses with and without causal model controls. — Allows controlled testing of the hypothesis under ideal conditions, clarifying whether the method itself is sufficient or if additional assumptions (e.g., correct model specification) are critical.

[PATH:empirical] Re-analysis of a well-known contradictory policy literature (e.g., minimum wage effects on employment) using a shared causal DAG and confounder control, with results compared to prior conflicting meta-analyses. — Provides a concrete, high-stakes test case; if the shared causal model yields consistent estimates across studies, it supports the hypothesis; if not, it suggests the method is insufficient.

C005.subject: Policy effectiveness
C005.object: bias correction uses a causal model of the bias-generating process, not just statistical pattern matching
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Policy effectiveness bias correction uses a causal model of the bias-generating process, not just statistical pattern matching]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative simulation study: apply causal-model-based bias correction (e.g., structural causal models with known bias mechanisms) vs. statistical-only methods (e.g., propensity score matching without causal graph) to synthetic policy evaluation data with known ground truth effects. — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing bias correction accuracy under controlled conditions where the causal structure of bias is known, isolating the role of causal modeling.

[PATH:empirical] Re-analysis of existing policy evaluations that used statistical bias correction (e.g., difference-in-differences with matching) but lacked a causal model of the bias-generating process; evaluate whether residual bias remains and whether adding a causal model would alter conclusions. — Provides real-world evidence on whether purely statistical methods are sufficient or whether causal models are necessary for reliable inference in policy settings.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal theoretical comparison: derive conditions under which statistical pattern matching alone can yield unbiased policy effect estimates (e.g., under exchangeability or ignorability) versus conditions requiring a causal model of the bias process. — Clarifies the logical boundaries of the hypothesis and identifies when it holds or fails, strengthening the evidential basis beyond simulation.

qualifier.temporal: when bias correction is applied in policy evaluation settings
qualifier.geographic: generalizable across contexts where causal structure of bias is identifiable
